mcqs.q: The incremental lines of Retzius represent:
opts: Successive layers of enamel laid down during crown formation
mcqs.explain: The lines of Retzius are brownish bands in ground section showing successive deposition of enamel during crown formation.

mcqs.q: In CROSS section, the lines of Retzius appear as:
mcqs.explain: In cross-section the lines of Retzius appear as concentric rings; in longitudinal section as oblique lines running DEJ → surface.

mcqs.q: The neonatal line is an accentuated incremental line that marks the:
mcqs.explain: The neonatal line marks the metabolic disturbance at birth and is seen in primary teeth and first permanent molars.

mcqs.q: Enamel tufts arise from:
opts: Abrupt changes in rod direction at the scalloped DEJ
mcqs.explain: Enamel tufts are branched, protein-rich (hypocalcified) structures arising from abrupt changes in the direction of groups of rods at the scalloped DEJ.

mcqs.q: The clinical significance of enamel TUFTS is that they:
mcqs.explain: Enamel tufts are thought to help prevent enamel fracture.

mcqs.q: Enamel LAMELLAE are clinically important because they:
opts: Provide a road of entry for bacteria, leading to caries
mcqs.explain: Enamel lamellae are leaf-like defects extending toward the DEJ that can act as a road of entry for bacteria, leading to caries.

mcqs.q: The dentino-enamel junction (DEJ) is described as:
opts: Scalloped, giving a firm hold of enamel to dentin
mcqs.explain: The DEJ is scalloped — shallow dentin depressions receive rounded enamel projections, ensuring a firm hold of enamel to dentin.

mcqs.q: Enamel spindles are:
opts: Odontoblast processes that cross the DEJ into the enamel
mcqs.explain: Enamel spindles are odontoblast processes that extend across the DEJ a short distance into the enamel.

mcqs.q: Prismless (structureless) enamel is:
opts: A 20–40 µm hypermineralized surface layer with crystals at right angles and no rods
mcqs.explain: Prismless enamel is a 20–40 µm thick, highly (hyper-) mineralized surface layer containing only crystals arranged almost at right angles to the surface.

mcqs.q: Perikymata are:
opts: Transverse surface grooves — the external manifestation of the lines of Retzius
mcqs.explain: Perikymata (imbrication lines) are transverse wave-like grooves on the enamel surface, representing the external manifestation of the incremental lines of Retzius.

mcqs.q: Enamel rod ends appear on the surface as:
opts: Concave depressions, shallower cervically and deeper near the incisal/occlusal surface
mcqs.explain: Enamel rod ends are concave depressions that are shallow at the cervical region and deepen toward the incisal/occlusal surface.

mcqs.q: Surface 'cracks' of enamel are actually the outer edges of:
mcqs.explain: Cracks are narrow fissure-like structures that are the outer edges of enamel lamellae.

mcqs.q: The delicate membrane (Nasmyth's membrane) covering a newly erupted tooth is the:
mcqs.explain: The enamel cuticle (Nasmyth's membrane) covers the crown of a newly erupted tooth and is soon removed by mastication.

mcqs.q: The enamel pellicle is:
opts: A salivary protein film that reforms within hours and can become a plaque site
mcqs.explain: The pellicle is a precipitate of salivary protein on erupted enamel; it reforms within hours and can be a site for microorganisms forming dental plaque.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, enamel appears:
opts: More radiopaque than other dental tissues
mcqs.explain: Because it is highly mineralized, enamel appears more radiopaque than other dental tissues.

mcqs.q: The most apparent AGE change in enamel is:
opts: Attrition (wear) of occlusal surfaces and proximal contacts
mcqs.explain: Attrition (wear) of occlusal surfaces and proximal contact points is the most apparent age change, with loss of vertical crown height.

mcqs.q: With age, the teeth typically become:
opts: Darker, more decay-resistant and less permeable
mcqs.explain: Age changes in the organic portion make teeth darker, may increase decay resistance, and reduce fluid permeability.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a HYPOCALCIFIED structure of enamel?
mcqs.explain: Hypocalcified (protein-rich) structures include rod sheaths, striations, DEJ, lines of Retzius, neonatal line, lamellae, tufts and spindles.

mcqs.q: Hunter-Schreger bands are produced by:
opts: Changes in the direction of rods, seen as alternating light/dark bands
mcqs.explain: Hunter-Schreger bands are alternating light and dark bands seen in ground sections under reflected light, due to changes in rod direction.

mcqs.q: Enamel lamellae extend:
opts: From the surface toward (or to) the DEJ
mcqs.explain: Enamel lamellae are leaf-like hypocalcified defects extending from the surface toward the DEJ, sometimes reaching dentin.

mcqs.q: Why is the scalloped shape of the DEJ functionally important?
opts: It interlocks enamel and dentin for a firm bond
It allows the pulp to expand
mcqs.explain: The scalloping interlocks the rounded enamel projections with the dentin depressions, ensuring a firm hold of enamel to dentin under masticatory forces.

saqs.q: List the hypocalcified structures of enamel.
saqs.a: Rod sheaths, striations, the DEJ, incremental lines of Retzius, the neonatal line, enamel lamellae, enamel tufts and enamel spindles.

saqs.q: Describe the lines of Retzius and the neonatal line.
saqs.a: Lines of Retzius: brownish incremental bands of enamel deposition — oblique lines (longitudinal), concentric rings (cross-section). The neonatal line is an accentuated line marking birth.

saqs.q: Contrast enamel tufts and enamel lamellae.
saqs.a: Tufts: branched, protein-rich, from rod-direction changes at the DEJ — prevent fracture. Lamellae: leaf-like defects from surface to DEJ — a route for bacteria → caries.

saqs.q: Describe the DEJ and enamel spindles.
saqs.a: The DEJ is scalloped — dentin depressions receive enamel projections for a firm hold. Enamel spindles are odontoblast processes crossing the DEJ into the enamel.

saqs.q: List the surface structures of enamel.
saqs.a: Prismless enamel (20–40 µm hypermineralized), perikymata (surface Retzius grooves), rod ends (concave), cracks, enamel cuticle (Nasmyth's), and the pellicle.

saqs.q: What is the enamel pellicle and its significance?
saqs.a: A precipitate of salivary protein on erupted enamel that reforms within hours; it provides a site for microorganisms → dental plaque.

saqs.q: Describe the age changes of enamel.
saqs.a: Attrition (wear) of occlusal/proximal surfaces → loss of vertical height and flattening; teeth become darker, more decay-resistant and less permeable.
